advisories: The story is written in English while the Spine and topic are in Turkish. No language requirement is stated, so this is not blocking, but it is worth confirming for a Turkish-language target.

Yasmin glimpses the tower's silhouette through a library window before BEAT_03, while the Spine says she has 'not yet seen' it and that it first enters her observation after she leaves. This is a mild tension. The story softens it with 'never really looked at before' and her later eyewitness view at the tower.
The atlas appears abruptly ('There was an atlas...') with no earlier scene-setting. It is consistent with the open obligations but slightly under-introduced for a 12-year-old reader.
The 'two lists' device at the tower is an effective way to separate observed from imagined, though it leans somewhat on explicit narration.
rationale: All five Spine beats are present in order and each is anchored to the right location. BEAT_01: she stops herself from fleeing, chooses to stay, and accepts that the Agreement has not closed. BEAT_02: she searches the library's known corners, finds no sign, and says 'I don't know whose it is' rather than inventing an owner. BEAT_03: she decides the library has nothing more to give and goes to the tower, keeping in mind that she can come back. BEAT_04: she separates what she sees (stone, door, eleven windows) from what she imagines (the atlas and its owner inside). The tower becomes a known place while the atlas and owner stay unknown. BEAT_05: she returns, recaps aloud, refuses to call the Agreement done, takes responsibility, and begins again knowing where to continue. The physical, spatial and temporal flow is coherent: the moon moves, and she travels out and back. Both open obligations remain open at the end, with no solved ending and no invented canon facts. Yasmin acts with real agency and makes choices at each decision point. The content is age-appropriate, and the imagery and the theme of honest uncertainty suit a 12-year-old. The only small deviation is the early silhouette sighting of the tower from the window, which is advisory only.
